doc.title: Pete Candoli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Integrated bands, the Esquire battle of bands and Stravinsky's Ebony Concerto
summary: Pete recalls Herman's band winning, the Esquire show, and the difficulties of playing Stravinsky's Ebony Concerto at the Paramount.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: When was the first time that you got into a band that was significantly integrated?

Well Woody’s band. I remember when we did, they had the Esquire magazine, the battle of the bands with Duke Ellington, who was the year before, I think ’45 was it, had won the Down Beat All Star Band, the pick of the band, and the following year, ’45 Woody won the band, Woody’s band, the Herman Herd. So we had the battle of the bands on

stage so to speak. And the narrator was Orson Welles. And then it was put on by Esquire magazine and I remember we were all individually introduced and then later on Woody had his own show with the Wildroot, and that’s when we premiered “Ebony Concerto” by Stravinsky, he had it written for us. I’ll tell you that episode sometime about Paramount Theater, what went on, rehearsing this music.
I guess that was pretty difficult, right? I mean you were playing shows?

Yeah it was difficult. Well I’ll tell you, it was difficult to play it correctly because playing it correctly I mean playing it with a certain finesse that’s required, but not hitting double D flats on the trumpet. You know I’m screaming above the band, six and eight shows a weekend at the Paramount. That is not conducive to playing delicate and with finesses. And the one part opens up with the woodwinds I guess, now this is Woody’s band [scats]. Then the fugue starts in. And at one point he had [scats] on guitar. Acoustic. And Don Lamond was on the band at that time instead of Davy Tough, and he was on the brush like [scats] now not sticks, brushes. And I came in on my high C [scats].
On your high C. Oh God.

You know the intervals are low. And so I said oh my God, I said, with a leather lip not geared for the finesse, but I knew it had to be, and in fact he conducted us in Los Angeles for the recording that we did with Woody’s band.
That must have been difficult for guys who were mostly used to reading swing music, to play the stuff that he wrote.
It was for certain people, like the clarinet part had a lot to be desired. I mean and guys that didn’t really read or have any legitimate training, it was very tough.
